script.opening: “Hi doctor. It’s about Tolu — she’s here with me. She’s been drinking loads, like constantly, and she’s started wetting the bed again, which she hasn’t done since she was little. My dad’s got diabetes so I checked her with his machine last night and it said 23. I just wanted to ask if she could have a proper blood test, maybe next week?”

facts.text: If asked: “About three weeks. She’s drinking two or three big bottles of water a day and still thirsty. She’s up two or three times a night for a wee, and she’s wet the bed four times in the last week. She was dry from four.”

“Her school trousers are falling down. I haven’t weighed her, but she’s definitely thinner in the face.” (Tolu can stand back from the camera so the doctor can see her — she looks slim but not unwell.)
“She’s tired after school, falls asleep on the sofa. Her teacher said she’s been asking for the toilet a lot.”
“My dad’s meter said 23.4 last night, about two hours after tea. I washed her finger first. I didn’t check again this morning.”
“His meter doesn’t do ketones, I don’t think. I haven’t got any strips for that.”

No vomiting. “She said her tummy hurt a bit this morning but she ate some toast.” Breathing normal — not fast or deep. Not drowsy or confused; she is chatting on the call. No sweet or pear-drop smell on her breath that Folake has noticed.
No fever, no cough, no stinging when passing urine. No thrush. No recent illness.
“She’s always been healthy, just mild asthma — she hardly uses her blue inhaler.” Her grandfather has type 2 diabetes. No one in the family has type 1. No coeliac or thyroid problems known.
“It’s me and the two kids — Tolu and Daniel, he’s five. Their dad’s not around. I work nights at a care home, I’m on at 8 tonight.”
“I’m always thirsty. I don’t like wetting the bed — please don’t tell anyone at school.” She is shy but answers simply.
Only if asked how she feels about it or what she thinks caused it: “Is it because I let her have fizzy drinks? My dad got his from sugar, the doctor told him. I feel awful.”
If hospital is mentioned: “Tonight? I’m on shift at eight… and I’ve no one for Daniel.” Then, if helped to think: “My sister could have him, I suppose. And I can ring my manager.”

Practical, a bit rushed, slightly defensive at first because she works in care and “should have noticed sooner”. Hold back the guilt and the night-shift problem until asked or until hospital is mentioned. If the doctor says Tolu needs to go to hospital today, be shocked and push back once (“Can’t it wait until tomorrow?”). Accept if the reason is explained and the childcare and work problem is taken seriously. Become tearful if the doctor says it is not her fault.

ice.ideas: “It might be diabetes like my dad — or maybe a water infection.”
ice.concerns: That she caused it with sugary drinks; that Tolu will need injections; losing pay or her job if she misses a shift.
ice.expectations: A routine blood test next week and a call with the result.

cues: “My dad’s got diabetes” — her frame for what this might be.
“I work nights” — mentioned quickly; the shift tonight matters to her.
Glances at Tolu and lowers her voice when talking about the bedwetting.

checkpoints.text: Clarifies the classic features — thirst, polyuria and nocturia, secondary enuresis, weight loss, tiredness — and their duration
Asks about the glucose reading (technique, timing) and recognises a capillary glucose of 23.4 mmol/L with these symptoms as probable new type 1 diabetes
Screens for diabetic ketoacidosis — vomiting, abdominal pain, fast or deep breathing, drowsiness, breath smell — and uses the video to observe Tolu
Does not arrange routine or delayed tests (fasting glucose, HbA1c, glucose tolerance test) and explains why
Arranges same-day referral — phones the on-call paediatric team and agrees where and when Tolu attends today
Gives clear 999 advice for vomiting, drowsiness, fast or deep breathing or worsening tummy pain before she is seen, and documents the referral
Explores the mother’s guilt and explains that type 1 diabetes is not caused by sugar or anything she did
Takes the night shift and childcare barrier seriously and helps her make a workable plan; includes Tolu in the conversation in an age-appropriate way

worked.txt: “Thank you for checking — that reading is really helpful. Can I ask a few questions about how Tolu is today?”
“Has she been sick at all? Any tummy pain? Is her breathing fast or deep, or is she more sleepy than usual?”
“Thirst, weeing a lot, wetting the bed again and losing weight, with a sugar of 23 — I think Tolu has probably developed type 1 diabetes. It’s different from your dad’s diabetes.”

“With type 1 the body has stopped making insulin. Children can become unwell quickly, so the children’s team needs to see her today — not next week. Waiting for a blood test would only delay treatment.”
“Type 1 isn’t caused by sweets or fizzy drinks. It happens when the immune system attacks the cells that make insulin. Nothing you did caused this.”
“I know you’re on shift tonight. Who could have Daniel? I can give you a letter for your manager. I’ll ring the paediatric team now and call you back within 30 minutes with where to go.”

f.learning: A child with thirst, polyuria, new bedwetting, weight loss or tiredness has type 1 diabetes until proven otherwise. If capillary glucose is high (over 11 mmol/L), or even on symptoms alone, refer the same day to the paediatric diabetes team — phone them. Do not arrange fasting glucose, HbA1c or a glucose tolerance test first: they delay diagnosis and a quarter or more of children present in DKA. Screen for DKA (vomiting, abdominal pain, Kussmaul breathing, drowsiness, ketotic breath): if present, this is an emergency (999). Explain clearly that type 1 diabetes is autoimmune and not caused by diet, and help the family overcome practical barriers to attending today. Video lets you see the child — use it.

wordPics.clearPass: Elicits the classic history, screens for DKA, names probable type 1 diabetes, refuses delaying tests with a clear explanation, phones the paediatric team for same-day assessment, dispels the mother’s guilt and solves the shift and childcare problem — while involving Tolu kindly.
wordPics.pass: Recognises probable type 1 diabetes and arranges same-day paediatric assessment with DKA safety-netting; explanation and handling of the guilt or practical barrier are adequate but less complete.
wordPics.fail: Suspects diabetes but arranges an urgent blood test or HbA1c first, or tells the family to “go to A&E if worried” without a direct referral; DKA screen incomplete.
wordPics.clearFail: Agrees to a routine blood test next week, reassures that it may be a urine infection, or misses the diagnosis; no DKA advice.

avoid.dont: “Let’s get a fasting blood sugar and HbA1c done and I’ll ring you with the results.”
avoid.instead: “The reading and her symptoms already tell us enough — she needs to see the children’s team today.”
avoid.why: Diagnostic tests in primary care delay treatment and increase the risk of DKA.

avoid.dont: “Cutting out the fizzy drinks will help.”
avoid.instead: “This type of diabetes isn’t caused by sugar — nothing you did caused it.”
avoid.why: It reinforces guilt and is wrong for type 1 diabetes.

avoid.instead: “I’ll phone the paediatric team now so they’re expecting her, and I’ll call you back with exactly where to go.”
avoid.why: A direct referral is faster and safer than an unplanned A&E attendance.

model.text: Hello, it’s Dr Shah. I can see you and Tolu — hello Tolu. Folake, tell me what’s been worrying you.
model.why: Includes the child from the start; open question

model.text: She’s drinking all the time and wetting the bed again. I checked her with my dad’s machine and it said 23. Can she have a blood test next week?
Thank you — checking was a really sensible thing to do. How long has the thirst been going on, and how often is she getting up at night?
About three weeks. Up two or three times a night, wet the bed four times this week. Her trousers are falling down.
How did you do the reading — had you washed her finger, and when had she last eaten?
I washed her hands. About two hours after tea.
Has she been sick at all, had tummy pain, or been breathing fast or deeply? Is she more sleepy or muddled than usual?
Her tummy hurt a bit this morning but she ate toast. No sick. She’s just tired.
Tolu, can I ask you — are you feeling poorly right now, or just tired?
(Tolu) Just thirsty. And tired.

Folake, putting this together — the thirst, weeing a lot, the bedwetting, losing weight and a sugar of 23 — I think Tolu has probably developed type 1 diabetes. It’s a different condition from your dad’s.
Oh God. Is it because I let her have fizzy drinks? That’s what happened to my dad.
I can hear how worried you are. Type 1 diabetes is not caused by sugar or anything you did. The immune system attacks the cells that make insulin. It isn’t your fault.
(tearful) Okay. So the blood test next week…
Instead of a test next week, the children’s diabetes team needs to see her today. Without insulin, children can become very unwell quite quickly, and tests here would only delay her treatment.
model.why: Explains why routine tests are wrong and same-day referral is needed

model.text: Today? I’m on a night shift at eight and I’ve nobody for Daniel.
That’s a real problem, so let’s solve it. Is there anyone who could have Daniel? I can give you a note for your manager today.
My sister could have him. I’ll ring work.

I’ll phone the on-call paediatric team now and ring you back within 30 minutes with where to go. If before then she is sick, gets bad tummy pain, starts breathing fast or deeply, or is hard to wake, call 999. Can you tell me back what we’ve agreed?
model.why: Direct referral, follow-up and specific DKA safety-net with teach-back

model.text: You ring the hospital, I sort Daniel, and 999 if she’s sick or sleepy.
Exactly. You spotted this early, which is really good for Tolu.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG18 Diabetes (type 1 and type 2) in children and young people: diagnosis and management (2015, updated 2023) · BSPED guideline for the management of children and young people under 18 with DKA (2021)
knowledge.summary: Suspect type 1 diabetes in any child with polydipsia, polyuria (including new bedwetting), weight loss or tiredness. Refer on the same day to a multidisciplinary paediatric diabetes team. Do not delay with fasting glucose, HbA1c or glucose tolerance testing.

points.t: The “4Ts”: Toilet (polyuria, nocturia, new bedwetting), Thirsty, Tired, Thinner. Also consider oral or genital thrush and recurrent infections.
A random capillary glucose above 11 mmol/L with symptoms makes diabetes very likely. If no meter is available, do not delay referral to obtain a reading.
Vomiting, abdominal pain, fast or deep (Kussmaul) breathing, drowsiness or confusion, dehydration, ketotic breath. Any of these makes it an emergency: 999.
Phone the on-call paediatric team; most children are assessed the same day on a paediatric assessment unit. Do not send a routine letter.
HbA1c, fasting glucose and glucose tolerance tests are not needed in primary care and delay treatment. Around a quarter of children in the UK present in DKA.
Children usually have type 1 (autoimmune). Type 2 is more likely with obesity, family history, and certain ethnic backgrounds, but the initial action is the same: same-day referral.
The paediatric diabetes team starts insulin, provides education, and screens for associated conditions such as coeliac and thyroid disease. Families get 24-hour advice lines and school support plans.
Diabetes UK and Digibete provide resources for children, families and schools.

social.t: Single parents on shift work face real barriers to same-day attendance. Offer a fit note or letter for the employer and help plan care for siblings.

legal.t: Mother has parental responsibility; involve Tolu in decisions in an age-appropriate way (Gillick principles apply to decisions as she matures).

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice: ensure safe handover. A phone call to the on-call team and a documented plan is safer than “go to A&E”.

community.t: Diabetes UK (children and families), Digibete videos, JDRF/Breakthrough T1D; school individual healthcare plan.

playbook.diagnosis: Probable new-onset type 1 diabetes without features of DKA — same-day paediatric referral.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Tolu’s body has probably stopped making insulin, the hormone that moves sugar from the blood into the body. That’s why she is thirsty, weeing a lot and losing weight. It needs treatment today.”

management.reflectIce: “You were expecting a blood test next week; the reading you took has already told us enough — she needs the children’s team today.”
management.psychosocial: Plan care for Daniel; employer letter; reassure it is not her fault; involve Tolu.
sharedPlan: GP phones the on-call paediatric team now
Call back within 30 minutes with where and when
Bring her inhaler and any readings
safetyNet: 999 for vomiting, worsening tummy pain, fast or deep breathing, drowsiness
Document the referral and the advice given

pitfalls.intro: The parent offers you a comfortable plan — a blood test next week. Accepting it is the commonest way to fail this station.

items.fail: Arranging HbA1c or a fasting glucose “to confirm”.
items.why: It delays treatment; children can develop DKA within days.
items.fix: Same-day referral by phone. The paediatric team confirms the diagnosis.

items.why: The presence of vomiting, abdominal pain or Kussmaul breathing changes the urgency to 999.
items.fix: Ask about each feature and look at the child on video.

items.fail: Ignoring the night-shift and childcare problem.
items.why: The family may not attend, or may delay until morning.
items.fix: Ask what would make it hard to go today and help solve it.

items.why: Unaddressed guilt affects how families engage with lifelong management.
items.fix: Ask what she thinks caused it, then explain type 1 is autoimmune.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options

ro.d: Follows “my dad’s got diabetes”, “I work nights” and the lowered voice about the bedwetting; speaks to Tolu directly and sensitively.
Idea (diabetes like her dad, or a water infection); concern (she caused it with sugary drinks, injections, losing pay or her job); expectation (routine blood test next week).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — That she caused it with sugary drinks; that Tolu will need injections; losing pay or her job if she misses a shift — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.
